content: Several therapeutic agents are currently employed to facilitate the clearance of airway secretions in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Mannitol, a sugar alcohol, has been shown to enhance mucociliary clearance, although its precise mechanism of action remains unclear. The dry powder formulation of mannitol offers a potentially more convenient alternative to traditional agents that require nebulization. Phase III clinical trials evaluating inhaled dry powder mannitol for cystic fibrosis treatment have been completed, and the drug is now available in Australia and certain European countries. This review updates prior evaluations of the therapy. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether inhaled dry powder mannitol is well-tolerated, whether it improves respiratory function and quality of life in individuals with cystic fibrosis, and to identify any associated adverse events. A comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register was conducted, with the last search performed on December 12, 2019. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing mannitol to placebo, other active inhaled treatments (e.g., hypertonic saline or dornase alfa), or no treatment. Six studies, encompassing 36 publications and involving 784 participants, were included in the analysis. Treatment durations ranged from 12 days to six months, with two studies incorporating an additional six-month open-label treatment phase. Five studies compared mannitol to control treatments (e.g., very low-dose or non-respirable mannitol), while one study compared mannitol to dornase alfa alone and to a combination of mannitol and dornase alfa. Two large parallel-design studies provided data for 600 participants, which allowed for pooled analysis of certain outcomes. The remaining studies had smaller sample sizes (22 to 95 participants) and could not be pooled due to differences in study design, interventions, and populations. The pooled evidence from the two large studies was assessed as being of low to moderate quality, while evidence from the smaller studies was judged to be of low to very low quality. All studies included an initial tolerance test for mannitol, and only participants who tolerated the drug were randomized. Consequently, the findings may not be generalizable to the broader cystic fibrosis population. Additional unpublished data were provided by the drug manufacturer and one study author to supplement the published data. In the pooled analysis of the two large studies, lung function, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) in both milliliters and percentage predicted, showed significant improvement in the mannitol group compared to the control group over a six-month period. This evidence was of moderate quality. These beneficial effects were observed in adult participants and in both users and non-users of concomitant dornase alfa. Smaller studies also demonstrated statistically significant improvements in lung function in the mannitol groups compared to non-respirable mannitol groups, but the quality of this evidence was low to very low. Regarding health-related quality of life, no consistent differences were observed between the mannitol and control groups across most domains, except for a reduced treatment burden in the mannitol group up to four months in the two pooled studies. However, this difference was not sustained at six months. It is important to note that the tool used to measure quality of life was not specifically designed for mucolytic therapies, and the pooling of age-appropriate tools in some studies may not be valid. As a result, the quality of evidence for quality-of-life outcomes was judged to be low to very low and should be interpreted with caution. The most commonly reported adverse events in both treatment groups included cough, hemoptysis, bronchospasm, pharyngolaryngeal pain, and post-tussive vomiting. When comparing adverse event rates between the mannitol and control groups, no statistically significant differences were observed, although some events may have clinical relevance for individuals with cystic fibrosis. In a 12-week crossover study involving 28 participants, comparisons of mannitol to dornase alfa alone and to a combination of mannitol and dornase alfa yielded very low-quality evidence. No statistically significant differences were observed in lung function or health-related quality of life. Cough was the most frequently reported side effect in the mannitol-alone group, while no cough was reported in the dornase alfa-alone group. Pulmonary exacerbations were the most common reason for withdrawal in the mannitol-plus-dornase alfa group. Evidence regarding secondary outcomes, such as pulmonary exacerbations, hospitalizations, symptoms, and sputum microbiology, was limited across all comparisons. No consistent statistically significant or clinically meaningful differences were observed between mannitol and control treatments, including dornase alfa. In conclusion, moderate-quality evidence suggests that mannitol treatment over six months is associated with improvements in certain measures of lung function in individuals with cystic fibrosis compared to control treatments. However, low to very low-quality evidence indicates no significant differences in quality of life between mannitol and control groups. Similarly, very low-quality evidence suggests no differences in lung function or quality of life when comparing mannitol to dornase alfa alone or to a combination of mannitol and dornase alfa. While mannitol may be considered as a treatment option for cystic fibrosis, further research is needed to identify the subgroups of patients who may derive the most benefit and to determine whether these benefits are sustained over the long term. Additionally, comparative studies evaluating the efficacy of mannitol against established mucolytic therapies are necessary before it can be widely adopted in clinical practice.
